prose.title: Gride Landed Amon-Ra St. Brown, Cash, and Eleventh Place
prose.dek: Matt Gerardi took the best player in one of the summer's biggest trades and got paid {{f.team.0003.trade_blind_bid_cash}} to do it. He still ranks {{f.team.0003.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}, because that trade cost him his quarterback, most of his auction money went on replacing him, and the backfield and tight end, both last in the league, got the scraps.

paragraphs: Amon-Ra St. Brown grades High-end WR1 and he is the reason to look at this roster at all. DJ Moore is a High-end WR3 next to him and the receiver room ranks {{f.team.0003.wr_rank|ord}} — which tells you what the rest of it looks like, because a High-end WR1 usually drags a room higher than that on his own.
Quarterback ranks {{f.team.0003.qb_rank|ord}} with Patrick Mahomes at Low-end QB1 and Malik Willis at Low-end QB2. Hold that thought. It becomes the story.

The backfield ranks {{f.team.0003.rb_rank}}, which is last, on Cam Skattebo at Mid RB2 and rookie Jadarian Price at Mid RB3, with Kimani Vidal filling a flex as a Replacement-level RB. Tight end also ranks {{f.team.0003.te_rank}}, also last, on Hunter Henry at Replacement-level TE. Two positions, both bottom of the league, and Deebo Samuel in the other flex as a Replacement-level WR.

The defense is mostly replacement-level, and it got {{f.team.0003.idp_auction_share}} of his auction money, a smaller share than anyone but Hawks and Sex Manther put there. Composite {{f.team.0003.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}, {{f.team.0003.studs_today}} studs, {{f.team.0003.holes_today}} holes.

April found him with {{f.team.0003.active_roster_opening}} active players, {{f.team.0003.holes_opening}} holes among the nine priced starting slots, not one top-twelve starter and {{f.team.0003.cap_opening}} already committed. Only Hawks also opened without a top-twelve starter, and they had more players for less money.

The trade with L.A. Looks brought in Amon-Ra St. Brown before the auction opened, which made DJ Moore his second-best receiver. The rest of the change came from elsewhere: Jadarian Price, the rookie from his May trade-up, had moved ahead of Chris Rodriguez in the backfield, and Michael Pittman was cut the day the auction rosters locked. The cost of the St. Brown deal was the quarterback. Sam Darnold went to L.A. Looks in the same trade, leaving Bryce Young, a Replacement-level QB, as the best quarterback he had and little behind him. He walked into the auction with {{f.team.0003.active_roster_preauction}} active players and {{f.team.0003.cap_preauction}} committed, the best offense he could assemble worth about half as much again as in April and his hole count exactly where it had started.

The auction filled both quarterback holes: Patrick Mahomes and Malik Willis gave him two quarterbacks worth starting where he had had one replacement-level one, and Hunter Henry moved ahead of an unranked David Njoku at tight end. He closed with {{f.team.0003.active_roster_current}} active players and a starting offense only modestly better than the one he took in; studs went from {{f.team.0003.studs_opening}} in April to {{f.team.0003.studs_postauction}}, holes from {{f.team.0003.holes_opening}} to {{f.team.0003.holes_postauction}}.

Those {{f.team.0003.holes_today}} holes are still there. He is carrying {{f.team.0003.cap_current_room}} of cap room, more than anyone but Hawks, against {{f.team.0003.cap_current_spent}} committed, so he can still act — which makes what he chose to buy the central question.

Nothing at the Expired Rookie Auction: {{f.team.0003.era_lots_won}} players, {{f.team.0003.era_spend}}, from a pool of {{f.league.era_pool_size}}. Fine. That pool sells players whose rookie deals ran out without earning a second one and its best player anywhere went for {{f.league.era_top_price}}.

The Free Agent Auction is where it gets strange. {{f.team.0003.faa_lots_won}} players for {{f.team.0003.faa_spend}}, and Patrick Mahomes alone took {{f.team.0003.top_buy_price}} of it — {{f.team.0003.top_buy_pct_of_spend}} of everything he spent. That is a defensible price for a Low-end QB1 in superflex and nobody would blink at it in isolation.

He also bought Malik Willis, for nearly as much again. Two quarterbacks, the two most expensive buys of his summer, while Bryce Young sat on an extension he had signed in May and Justin Fields came in at the minimum for good measure. Five quarterbacks, counting Shedeur Sanders from the St. Brown trade. The room ranks {{f.team.0003.qb_rank|ord}}.

What that left for everything else was fourteen buys at the league minimum. Hunter Henry, Jake Tonges, Jalen Tolbert, CJ Daniels, Brenen Thompson, Colbie Young, and a defensive unit assembled for {{f.team.0003.idp_auction_spend}} in total. A last-ranked tight end room and a last-ranked backfield were the price of paying twice over at quarterback after trading his starter away.

Measured against the money, it was a thin return. He spent {{f.team.0003.faa_off_spend}} on offense at the Free Agent Auction, and for what that money bought he ranks {{f.team.0003.faa_off_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}. Room to improve was not the problem: nobody took more holes into the auction. Hawks took in as many, spent a little more and got far more for every dollar; CBP, in his own division, spent more than half as much again and did better still on the improvement itself.

t.0003.faa_value.title: Who got the most for his money

captions.t.0003.faa_value: Ranked by how much each owner's starting offense improved between the auction lock and the close, for every dollar he spent on quarterbacks, backs, receivers and tight ends at the Free Agent Auction.

paragraphs: {{f.team.0003.contracts_count}} contract moves, {{f.team.0003.trades_count}} trades, {{f.team.0003.roster_removals_total}} removals. The trades are the interesting half and they come in two very different flavors.

Four of the five are pick shuffling, all inside two days in late May, and he came out of it with {{f.team.0003.rookie_picks_count}} rookie picks — more than anyone. He moved up to 1.04 and took Jadarian Price, who is already a Mid RB3 and started Week One. He turned a 2027 second into 2.09 and 4.12. He spun 3.06 into 3.09 and 3.12. It is real work and it produced real players, though the cost was Travis Etienne, whom he had tagged only two days earlier and then sent to Real Deal Creel with 1.07 to move up three slots.

The fifth is the one that matters. He sent Sam Darnold, Jalen Coker and Emmett Johnson to L.A. Looks and received Amon-Ra St. Brown, Shedeur Sanders and {{f.team.0003.trade_blind_bid_cash}} of blind-bid money. He gave up three players who together are worth less than half of St. Brown alone, and the other franchise paid him cash on top. On value, he won it going away; the bill arrived later, at quarterback.

The contracts are less impressive. Bryce Young was extended in May and now sits on the bench at Replacement-level QB carrying a salary that would be a starting quarterback's on most of these rosters. Mahomes was signed to a multi-year deal and restructured the same day, two operations for one contract. Travis Etienne was tagged and then immediately traded, which is a lot of process for a player he did not keep.

The removals carry a warning worth stating plainly. Michael Pittman was cut at a salary of real size and the penalty attached to it has no charge year stamped on it yet, so {{f.team.0003.cuts_penalty_unstamped}} of cap consequence is sitting in the ledger unassigned. Nothing has hit this season — {{f.team.0003.cuts_penalty_2026}} — and {{f.team.0003.cuts_penalty_2027_deferred}} is formally deferred, but that unstamped figure is not a rounding error and it is going to land somewhere.

The rookie class is deep and unproven. Jordyn Tyson at 1.05 and Chris Bell at 2.03 sit in the two strongest historical bands of his own class and both grade Replacement-level WR so far. Anthony Hill Jr. at 4.12 is already starting at linebacker with no NFL season behind him, which is not a grade on him — nobody can price him yet — so much as a statement about what is behind him.

He is {{f.team.0003.division_rank|ord}} of {{f.team.0003.division_size}} in his division, behind Blake Bombers and CBP, and he plays each of them five times. Those ten games decide his seed, and he is the underdog in all of them.

Strongest team in the league? No — {{f.team.0003.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}. Best offseason? Genuinely closer than the rank suggests, and this is the honest tension in his summer: he made one of the best individual moves of the summer, acquiring a High-end WR1 and cash for three players who do not add up to him, and he built {{f.team.0003.rookie_picks_count}} rookie picks out of a pile of swaps. Then he spent {{f.team.0003.faa_spend}} at auction, most of it on two quarterbacks to refill the position that same trade had emptied.

The biggest advantage is Amon-Ra St. Brown, full stop, and Patrick Mahomes is the only other offensive starter here who ranks in the top twelve at his position. The biggest weakness is everything around them: a receiver room that ranks {{f.team.0003.wr_rank|ord}} even with St. Brown in it, a quarterback room that still ranks {{f.team.0003.qb_rank|ord}} despite the money, and last in the league at both running back and tight end. The thin defense is the cheapest of his problems to fix.

For the little it is worth this early — {{f.league.wk_teams_final}} NFL teams had played when this was written — his two finished starters banked {{f.team.0003.wk_points_final}} points between them. Jadarian Price, the rookie he traded up for, was the better of the two. Hunter Henry, bought at the league minimum, was barely behind him. None of his quarterbacks had played yet.
